schools.summary: Gill cannot date the instruction, borrows Josephus for the trumpets' dimensions — barely a cubit long, a narrow tube widening at the mouthpiece and finishing in a bell — records the Targum of Jonathan's claim that Moses bore the cost himself while judging the treasury likelier, and hears the gospel in the metal. Calvin files the ordinance under the First Commandment: Israel was to be set moving by these blasts so that nothing might be undertaken in war or peace except under divine auspices, the three uses being convocation, war and festival. He defends the seeming indignity of priestly trumpeters — the office was no servile errand but set them over public business, lest the multitude convene tumultuously in blind and headlong passion, and testified that every assembly God did not preside over stood accursed.

Henry thinks the trumpets much like our own in outline, contrasts the two here with the hundred and twenty at Solomon's dedication, and finds the divine authorship of so small a matter the most striking thing about it — ordinary prudence might have suggested trumpets without any revelation, yet Israel's constitution was to be divine throughout.

Clarke raises the practical difficulty that two instruments seem far too few for so vast an army and answers that those within earshot moved first and taught the rest in succession; he suspects the pair differed in length and width and so in pitch, reports Josephus as keeping one for the nobles and the other for the congregation, and notes that Joshua's seven trumpets were of rams' horns. Wesley observes that the tally rose afterwards as the priestly families multiplied.

Ellicott corrects 'of a whole piece' to beaten or turned work, supposes the instruments straight like the one on Titus's arch rather than crooked like the keren, and argues from vocabulary that these were new: Leviticus uses shophar of the jubilee trumpet, whereas hazozerah appears here for the first time.

debates: How the two summonses were told apart. Gill and Henry make the difference numerical — one trumpet for the princes, both for the congregation; Clarke, citing Josephus, supposes instead two instruments of different length and pitch, one reserved for the nobles and one for the people, so that the tone itself declared which summons it was.

3.pericope_label: The signals: assembly, alarm and march

schools.summary: Gill describes the summoning note as even and continuous on both instruments, hears the alarm as broken, uneven and quavering — reaching for the old onomatopoeia tara-tan-tara — and fixes the venue of the convocation at the entrance of the tent, the people gathering rather than moving off in separate bodies.

Clarke agrees the alarm was rough, short sharp notes closing with long ones on both trumpets, and thinks the resemblance of teruah to the Roman taratantara suggests a clarion's blare; he reconstructs the missing arithmetic of the signals — one alarm for the east, two for the south, three presumably for the west and four for the north — and reports at length the evidence for and against the Greek supplement. Wesley reads the phrase about journeys as making each blast a signal for one squadron to advance and the rest to follow.

Ellicott hesitates over whether the clause means with one trumpet, but once, or at the same time; holds teruah to be a loud unbroken blast distinguished from the convocation signal by volume and continuity; notes that the marching order was given more fully two chapters earlier and that only the eastern and southern camps are prescribed here; and presses the practical moral that the gospel trumpet must never yield an uncertain sound. Keil and Delitzsch draw the contrast at the level of the verbs, one denoting short sharp bursts and the other a sustained peal.

debates: What the alarm sounded like. Gill and Clarke hear something broken, uneven and quavering, likening it to the Roman taratantara; Ellicott holds teruah to be a loud and continuous blast, distinguished from the summons precisely by its unbroken character; Keil and Delitzsch place the contrast in the verbs instead, one meaning short sharp tones and the other a sustained peal.
outliers: Houbigant judged the Greek supplement about a third and fourth alarm so necessary that he printed the Latin in his own text and supplied Hebrew for it beneath, supposing the words original but lost to a copyist. Clarke reports the counter-evidence honestly: neither the Samaritan nor any version but the Coptic acknowledges the sentence, and the collations of Kennicott and De Rossi turn up nothing to support it.

8.pericope_label: The priests to blow: war and festival

schools.summary: Gill counts two blowers because Aaron had two sons, cites Maimonides for the rule that the number never fell below two nor rose above a hundred and twenty, defines the oppressor as an invader who besieges cities and distresses the inhabitants, and takes the day of gladness for any extraordinary deliverance turned into rejoicing. Calvin gets the sharpest point from the festivals: God thereby made plain that he approved no feast and accepted no sacrifice unless his own command went before it, and because men are forever daring in their innovations he would have the lawful observance ratified by trumpet-blast, as though he published the holy assemblies through priestly mouths. He also prefers 'your prosperities' to the usual rendering of the second offering, and explains the memorial as God looking upon them with fatherly favour when they assemble at his command.

Clarke reads the war-summons as convening deliberation and prayer together, and concludes that whenever Israel decamped, encamped, fought or kept festival at God's appointment they might look for both his presence and his blessing. Wesley adds the condition without which the ceremony is empty — they shall be saved if they use the ordinance trusting and depending upon God for help — and says in a sentence that God takes pleasure in our religious exercises when we take pleasure in them.

Ellicott qualifies the priestly monopoly from the later histories, where Levites and perhaps others handle the hazozerah, traces the practice through Phinehas in the Midianite war and Abijah's address to Jeroboam, and marks the exception at Jericho, where the circling priests bore the ram's horn instead. Keil and Delitzsch explain why the manner of use as well as the manufacture came under divine prescription, and distinguish the idiom for entering upon war from the phrase used elsewhere for marching out to battle.

11.pericope_label: The cloud taken up; Israel leaves Sinai

schools.summary: Gill dates the departure to the twentieth of Ijar and reckons the stay at twelve months less ten days, and makes the mechanism of the command explicit — it came in the lifting of the cloud. Calvin weighs Israel's compliance and finds it short-lived: they deserve praise for setting out promptly, and the march was only three days, yet even that harassed and wearied them, and presently their levity and inconstancy showed itself. He also disputes Jerome's rendering of the repeated noun as 'troops', since its root is the verb beside it and Scripture uses it consistently for halting-places.

Henry hears in the Samaritan's inserted sentence a warning against lingering — Sinai gendereth to bondage and stands for the law, a schoolmaster bringing us to Christ in which no one may settle down — describes the labour of striking every tent, and finds a purpose in the chapter's insistence that they moved at the Lord's commandment: it forestalls the slander that Israel wandered so long because they had lost themselves. Those who surrender to the guidance of God's word and Spirit hold a steady course even when they appear bewildered. Every removal here, he concludes, is only from one wilderness into another, and rest belongs to heaven.

Clarke makes the encampment eleven months and twenty days, notices the sentence the Samaritan copy inserts at this junction, counts three stations between Sinai and Paran, and admits how hard identification is, since one often cannot tell whether a site lies forward of the last or behind it. Wesley observes that Israel afterwards travelled elsewhere and came back to Paran.

Ellicott computes eleven months and nineteen days and then undercuts his own figure, since Exodus names no day of the third month and he will not lean on the tradition dating the law fifty days after the exodus; he suspects the spot intended is Kibroth-hattaavah and sketches the limits of the Paran desert. Keil and Delitzsch treat the verse as a heading rather than narrative, the statement that the cloud settled in Paran summarising a whole journey whose particulars follow later, Paran being the third station and not the first.

debates: How long Israel lay encamped at Sinai. Gill reckons twelve months less ten days on Jewish authority, Clarke eleven months and twenty days, Ellicott eleven months and nineteen days — and Ellicott then unsettles all three by pointing out that Exodus never names the day of the month on which they arrived.

schools.summary: Calvin lays out the whole formation — four hosts, each headed by a tribe with two under it, ringing the sanctuary at every halt and marching with the Levites interspersed, the ark going before the column so that all might follow the more confidently — and reads the placements through Jacob's dying oracle: Judah's precedence anticipates the prophecy, Reuben's second rank softens his disgrace, Manasseh's subordination to Ephraim fulfils another clause, and Dan's standard answers the word that Dan should judge his people. Unless Reuben and Manasseh had been persuaded their demotion came by divine command, jealousy would never have let them submit calmly to their natural inferiors. Gill hears the same note, Judah leading because the Messiah was to spring from it, and plays on Reuben's name — behold the son — since with the tabernacle before that division and the holy things behind it, whichever way it faced it had a type of Christ in view.
Clarke sets the whole order of march out as a bare table.

Ellicott fixes the Levites' place most precisely: Gershonites with two wagons and Merarites with four went immediately behind Judah's division so as to have time to raise the dwelling before the Kohathites arrived with the sacred things, after which came Reuben's division, then the Kohathites in the centre, then Ephraim's, then Dan's as rearguard — a sequence which explains the psalm praying God to stir up his strength before Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh.

Gill fixes the Kohathite position between Reuben's standard and Ephraim's, defends Dan's place at the tail as fittest because that division was the most populous after Judah, and prefers a second sense for the word usually rendered rearward — gatherer-up of all the camps, under whose protection came males below twenty, women, children, the sick, the mixed multitude and any who straggled. Following Jarchi he treats the closing verse as describing a settled practice rather than one day's movement, totals the four divisions at 186,400, 151,450, 108,100 and 157,600, and sees in the whole spectacle the church militant walking by gospel order.

Wesley explains why the two Levite contingents travelled so far apart: Gershon and Merari moved off directly behind the leading camp and kept a good interval ahead of Kohath, so as to have the dwelling ready to receive its furniture when the Kohathites came up later.
Ellicott prefers to read the closing words as a plain statement, and they set forward, rather than as a temporal clause.

Calvin calls it a gross error to identify Hobab with Jethro, who had gone home days after his visit: decrepit age suits ill with such labours, Moses at eighty was far younger than his father-in-law, and Judges settles it by showing Hobab's descendants alive in Canaan. He also generalises the refusal — Hobab shows the whole race in a mirror, longing for what the carnal senses grasp, since men naturally prefer their own country however barren, as the proverb about the rocky Ithaca attests — while allowing that the request was no feint, since Moses prevailed only after persevering entreaty.

Henry takes Hobab for Jethro's son, left with Moses as Barzillai left Chimham with David, and notes that one Hebrew word covers both father-in-law and brother-in-law. He hears Moses staking everything on a promise and draws the rule that pilgrims bound for the heavenly Canaan should invite their friends along, since we lose none of the covenant's treasures by others sharing them; the refusal he blames on affection for native soil unchecked by any believing regard for the promise — Hobab sprang from Abraham's loins but was no heir of Abraham's faith.

Clarke suspects the whole episode stands out of its chronological place, and makes the invitation a test of religion itself: true religion is always benevolent, those who know most of God's goodness are readiest to invite others into it, and a religion that shuts out of salvation everyone who will not hold a particular creed or worship in a particular way is not of God. Wesley reasons that Raguel, Reuel and Jethro are one man under three names, so Hobab must be his son, young enough for such travelling where his father was not.

Ellicott argues from syntax that Hobab, not Jethro, is the relation named here, as Judges confirms, and that the cognate noun may mean brother-in-law; against those who make Zipporah Hobab's daughter he urges chronology, since a man past eighty would seek his guide among Zipporah's own generation rather than the one above hers. He reads the invitation as a standing lesson to the Christian church, whose members are bound and privileged alike to pass on the summons they have obeyed.

debates: Who Hobab was. Calvin, Wesley and Henry all take him for Jethro's son, arguing from Jethro's age and departure and from the survival of Hobab's descendants in Canaan; Ellicott argues from Hebrew syntax and from Judges that Hobab himself is the relation named here, though the term may mean brother-in-law rather than father-in-law, and rejects on chronological grounds the view that Zipporah was Hobab's daughter.

30.pericope_label: Hobab's refusal and Moses' second plea

schools.summary: Gill calls the answer peremptory but thinks Hobab probably changed his mind afterwards, like the son in the parable, and notes that the pledge which follows is stated twice over to confirm it. Calvin reads the crucial clause backwards and accuses everyone else of missing it: where others translate simply 'for thou hast known', as though Moses wanted Hobab retained for Israel's convenience, Calvin insists the Hebrew carries more than one causal particle, so that Hobab had already served them as eyes and borne many inconveniences precisely in order to receive his recompense — the plea being not 'be our eyes hereafter' but 'do not throw away what your labour has earned'.

Clarke argues from Judges and Samuel, where Hobab's descendants appear settled among Israel, that he either relented or returned; he answers the objection that a guide was superfluous beside the pillar by distinguishing the general marches, which the cloud directed, from the particular excursions parties made while the main army lay still, for which a man who knew where water and fuel lay was needed — what men cannot do for themselves God does by special mercy, and what he has qualified a man to do he leaves that man to do. Wesley allows Hobab may have spoken sincerely and been overcome later, and lists what local knowledge would supply: water for the cattle, and warning of serpents, wild beasts and hostile neighbours.

Ellicott concedes the narrative never says whether Hobab went, thinks the renewed solicitation most probably succeeded, and rests on the certainty that the Kenites as a body went up with Judah and dwelt among the people; he draws the general principle that for all the guidance vouchsafed from heaven Moses neglected none of the ordinary precautions a leader owes his people.

debates: What 'thou mayest be to us instead of eyes' means. Clarke, Wesley and Ellicott read it prospectively, as asking Hobab to supply desert knowledge the cloud did not cover; Calvin reads it retrospectively, holding that the Hebrew's doubled causal particle makes it a reminder that Hobab has already been their eyes and would forfeit his recompense by leaving now.

33.pericope_label: Three days' journey; the ark and the cloud

schools.summary: Gill explains the title mount of the Lord from the descent and the giving of the law, quoting the Targums, and breaks the three days' journey into separated stages — Taberah for a month, Hazeroth for seven days, then Paran — noting that the Targum of Jonathan's thirty-six miles cannot be reconciled with Bunting's eight. He also widens the cloud beyond the sanctuary, spreading it over the whole body of the people as a screen from the sun's heat. Calvin agrees on the mountain's name, holding the title properly imposed after the law to inspire lasting reverence, but understands a continuous three-day march, since no tents were pitched until Paran and the people slept in the open air; the ark, he says, was not sent three days ahead but so placed in the van that when the cloud settled they halted at a station God had prescribed.

Henry marks the leave-taking: they departed from the mountain where they had seen God's glory and been taken into covenant, never to see such appearances constantly, and Scripture scarcely mentions Sinai again except in retrospect.

Clarke resolves the ark's position by sequence rather than place — the Kohathites carried it in the centre, but since the army never stirred until the cloud lifted, the ark is said to go before as the first thing to move. Wesley separates camp from column, adds that the ark could not have served as a visible guide anyway since it went on men's shoulders, and makes the cloud over it a single token of God's presence with it; the phrase about searching out a resting-place he calls frankly metaphorical, and he turns the omission of night in the next verse into a rule of reading, that we must supply out of one passage what another leaves out.

Ellicott lays both sides of the ark question out before choosing: the Kohathite charge and their place behind the second camp suggest the midst, and the cloud may have spread over the whole host rather than resting on the ark alone; yet the natural sense of the verse is that the ark went in front, confirmed by Exodus, Deuteronomy and the Jordan crossing, where Israel was told to follow after it. He will not conclude that its place was uniform on every march.

debates: Whether the three days ran consecutively. Calvin understands a continuous march with no tents pitched until Paran; Gill separates the stages, placing a month at Taberah and seven days at Hazeroth between them, and appeals to Bunting's eight miles against the Targum's thirty-six.

Where the ark travelled. Clarke and Wesley keep it in the centre of the column and explain the language of going before by its being first to move, or by the cloud above it; Calvin and Ellicott place it literally in the van, Ellicott resting on the Jordan crossing where Israel was expressly told to go after it.
outliers: Ibn Ezra held that this particular three days' journey differed from all the others precisely in where the ark was carried, which would leave the apparent conflict between this verse and the marching order without any need of harmonising.

35.pericope_label: Rise up, Lord; return, O Lord

schools.summary: Gill offers three constructions of the prayer at the halt: that God would take up his abode among them and manifest his mercy; or, rendered actively, that he would return the thousands of Israel to the land sworn to their fathers, which is Ben Gersom's reading; or that he would turn those thousands into myriads and multiply them tenfold, as the Jerusalem Targum takes it. Calvin explains why a war-cry was needed at every departure, the march being anything but peaceful, and makes much of Moses calling the enemies God's rather than Israel's — victory could be the more confidently expected with the righteous avenger defending his own quarrel, and it was no slight comfort to learn that whoever harassed them unjustly had made an enemy of the God who guards his people as the apple of his eye. In the second prayer he finds a pastoral purpose, since the halts did the people good, God then showing his care of them as the head of a family does at home.

Clarke puts the necessity bluntly — unless God arose and scattered his enemies there was no hope of Israel getting through the wilderness, and unless he went first they could not safely follow — dates the second prayer to the moment the divisions halted to pitch, notes that the Hebrew is literally the ten thousand thousands, and thinks the sixty-eighth psalm composed with reference to this history.

Keil and Delitzsch record the words as evidence of Moses' joyous confidence and as encouragement to the congregation, explaining that he could speak so because he knew Jehovah and the ark to be inseparable and saw in the ark, as God's throne, a material pledge of the Almighty's gracious presence.

debates: What 'Return, O Lord, unto the many thousands of Israel' asks. Gill canvasses three senses — that God would dwell among them, that he would bring the thousands back to the promised land (Ben Gersom), or that he would multiply them into myriads (the Jerusalem Targum) — without settling between them.
